title: What can two documents establish?
subtitle: The Zimmermann telegram and Wilson’s use of it
summary: Compare a conditional diplomatic proposal with a public argument. Decide what the documents say, what you infer, and what this pair cannot establish.
audience: General readers; no prior history course required.
scope: United States–Germany–Mexico, 1917. A small source pair, not a complete explanation of US entry into the war.

sources.title: Decoded Zimmermann telegram
sources.creator: Arthur Zimmermann; displayed in the archive’s English decoded-message transcript

rights.basis: Two short attributed phrases (15 words total) for close critical comparison; original surrounding paraphrase. No full translation or scan reproduced.
rights.scope: US local prototype; wider distribution requires release-specific review.

sources.title: Wilson’s address to Congress
sources.locator: Transcript, paragraph beginning “But they have played their part”; RG 46
sources.creator: Woodrow Wilson

rights.basis: Short attributed quotation from an official presidential address; US government text. No facsimile or modern editorial copy reproduced.
rights.scope: US local prototype; wider distribution requires release-specific review.

passages.title: A condition, not an accomplished alliance
passages.text: In the event of this not succeeding
passages.context: The preceding sentence states an aim to keep the United States neutral. The proposal is introduced as conditional on that aim failing. The diplomatic recipient is being instructed; this is not a reply from Mexico.

passages.title: Terms proposed
passages.text: make war together, make peace together
passages.context: The message proposes cooperation and support. A proposal is evidence of what the sender offers, not evidence that the recipient accepts.

passages.title: A public argument
passages.text: That it means to stir up enemies against us at our very doors
passages.context: Wilson immediately identifies the intercepted note to the German minister in Mexico City as evidence. This passage addresses Congress and argues that the German government threatens US security.

claims.text: The telegram introduces a conditional proposal.
claims.qualification: A proposal does not establish acceptance.

claims.text: Wilson uses the intercepted message in a public security argument.
claims.qualification: An interpretation of the speech’s use of evidence, not proof of the speech’s effect on every listener.

context: The decoded message is presented in English by the National Archives. Its German original and the entire interception/decoding chain are not part of this exercise.
The speech refers to the intercepted message. It is dependent evidence for the message, while being direct evidence of Wilson’s public argument.
Neither source supplies Mexico’s reply. Neither isolates the telegram from the other causes of the US war decision.

prompts.claim: The message makes the proposed cooperation conditional.
prompts.feedback: The quoted conditional phrase directly supports this classification. The editorial context explains what the condition refers to. An offer under a condition does not establish a completed agreement.
Neither selected document supplies a Mexican acceptance. Missing evidence does not prove rejection either.

prompts.claim: The border-threat wording could help frame war as a response to danger.
prompts.feedback: This is a defensible interpretation of the rhetoric. The wording alone does not measure its effect on Congress or the public.

prompts.claim: The telegram alone caused the US declaration of war.
prompts.feedback: This pair cannot isolate a single cause. A speech’s use of one document is not a controlled account of all causes.

activity.transfer: A later newspaper repeats the telegram. Does that automatically give you an independent confirmation? Explain what you would need to know about its source.
rubric: Distinguish a record from an independent source of its information.
Name one missing perspective or link in provenance.
Attach the limitation to a specific claim.

reviewLimitations: Screen-reader and learner sessions have not been performed.
